nodes.name: Quantum parameter $q$
nodes.statement: Let $q=e^{\pi ib^2}$ be the quantum parameter.

nodes.name: Alternative names of $G_b(z)$
nodes.statement: The quantum dilogarithm function $G_b(z)$, defined for $b\in \R_{>0}$, is also known as the quantum exponential function or the hyperbolic gamma function.

nodes.name: Faddeev's variant $\Phi_b(z)$
nodes.statement: It bears its name from the properties of its variants $g_b(z)$ and $\Phi_b(z)$ given by \Eq{\Phi_b(z)=g_b(e^{2\pi bz}) = \frac{\over[\ze_b]}{G_b(\frac{Q}{2}-iz)},}
nodes.statement_short: Defines the variant $\Phi_b(z)$ as $g_b(e^{2\pi bz})$, equal to $\over[\ze_b]/G_b(\frac{Q}{2}-iz)$.

nodes.name: The constants $Q$ and $\ze_b$
nodes.statement: where $Q=b+b\inv$ and $\ze_b=e^{\frac{\pi i}{2}(\frac{b^2+b^{-2}}{6}+\frac{1}{2})}$

nodes.name: Pentagon relation for Heisenberg type operators
nodes.statement: Using $\Phi_b(z)$, the pentagon relation can be written formally for the Heisenberg type operator $[p,x]=~\frac{1}{2\pi i}$ as well by \Eq{\Phi_b(p)\Phi_b(x)=\Phi_b(x)\Phi_b(p+x)\Phi_b(p),} where we ignored the concerns of unboundedness and self-adjointness of operators.
nodes.statement_short: Formal pentagon identity $\Phi_b(p)\Phi_b(x)=\Phi_b(x)\Phi_b(p+x)\Phi_b(p)$ for Heisenberg operators.

nodes.name: $q$-binomial formula
nodes.statement: On the other hand, the appearance of $G_b(z)$ in the $q$-binomial formula \cite{BT, Ip1} given by \Eq{(u+v)^{it} = b\int_{\R+i0}\frac{G_b(ib\t-ibt)G_b(-ib\t)}{G_b(-ibt)}u^{i \t}v^{i (t-\t)} d\t,} where $uv=q^2vu$ as above, suggests that $G_b(bz)$ serves as the quantum analogue of the classical Gamma function.
nodes.statement_short: Integral $q$-binomial expansion of $(u+v)^{it}$ whose kernel is built from $G_b$.

nodes.name: Aim of the paper
nodes.statement: This paper atempts to relate all these functions to the present choice of Teschner's definition of $G_b(z)$ in \cite{BT} so that the graphical presentations for this function can be translated to all these variants by shifting, stretching and phase changes easily.

nodes.name: Complex coloring method (Jan Homann)
nodes.statement: We adopt the coloring method for a complex function developed by Jan Homann. The color function is obtained from the Mathematica code by Axel Boldt and can be found in \cite{AB}. In short, given a complex valued function defined on the complex plane, we represent the function by coloring the complex plane according to the following rules. The argument of a complex value is encoded by the hue of a color (red = positive real, and then counterclockwise through yellow, green, cyan, blue and purple; cyan stands for negative real). The absolute value of the function is represented by the brightness and saturation of the color: strong colors denote points close to the origin, with black = 0, weak colors denote points with large absolute value, with white = $\oo$.
nodes.statement_short: Represent a complex function by hue = argument and brightness/saturation = modulus.
nodes.genus: coloring method for a complex function
differentia: The argument of a complex value is encoded by the hue of a color
The absolute value of the function is represented by the brightness and saturation of the color

nodes.name: Hue-saturation-brightness color function
nodes.statement: The color is defined by 3 numbers ranging from 0 to 1. In the present coding, at the point $z=x+iy$ with value $f=f(x+iy)$, they are explicitly given by \Eq{Hue[h,s,b]:=\{\frac{Arg(f)}{2\pi}, \frac{1}{1+0.3 \ln(|f|+1)}, 1-\frac{1}{1.1+5\ln(|f|+1)}\},} where $h$ stands for hue, $s$ the saturation and $b$ the brightness.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit HSB triple: hue $=Arg(f)/2\pi$, saturation and brightness logarithmic in $|f|$.

nodes.name: Effect of taking inverse on the coloring
nodes.statement: The color function is hence given by Figure \ref{color}. We also note that taking inverse amounts to flipping the brightness of the color, and taking the opposite hue along the imaginary direction.

nodes.name: Brightness reference $f(z)=e^z$
nodes.statement: A good reference for the brightness of the color is given by the exponential function $f(z)=e^z$, see Figure \ref{exp}.

nodes.name: The graph of $f(z)=z^3$
nodes.statement: From Figure \ref{z3}, we observe that for $f(z)=z^3$ it has an order 3 zero, with the hue of color cycling around the point $z=0$ for 3 times.

nodes.name: The graph of the Gamma function $f(z)=\G(z)$
nodes.statement: From Figure \ref{Gamma} for $f(z)=\G(z)$, we observe the phase change behavior and the exponential growth along the imaginary direction. The few bright spot at $z=-n,n\in\Z_{\geq0}$ indicates the simple poles.

nodes.name: The graph of the Riemann Zeta function $f(z)=\ze(z)$
nodes.statement: From Figure \ref{zeta} for $f(z)=\zeta(z)$, we observe the existence of nontrivial zeros along the line $Re(z)=~\frac{1}{2}$, the trivial zeroes at $z=-2n,n\in\Z_{\geq1}$ (where the color lines come together), the pole at $z=1$, and the limit $\dis\lim_{Re(z)\to+\oo}\ze(z)=1$.

nodes.name: Barnes' double Zeta function
nodes.statement: Let $\w:=(w_1,w_2)\in \C^2$. The double Zeta function is defined as \Eq{\ze_2(s,z|\w):=\sum_{m_1,m_2\in\Z_{\geq0}}(z+m_1w_1+m_2w_2)^{-s}.}

nodes.name: Barnes' double Gamma function
nodes.statement: The double Gamma function is defined as \Eq{\G_2(z|\w):=\exp\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial s}\ze_2(s,z|\w)|_{s=0}\right).}

nodes.name: $\G_b(x)$
nodes.statement: Let \Eq{\G_b(x):=\G_2(x|b,b\inv).}

nodes.name: The quantum dilogarithm $S_b(x)$
nodes.statement: The quantum dilogarithm is defined as the function: \Eq{S_b(x):=\frac{\G_b(x)}{\G_b(Q-x)},} where $Q=b+b\inv$.

nodes.name: The quantum dilogarithm $G_b(x)$
nodes.statement: The main object of study is the variant given by \Eq{G_b(x):=e^{\frac{\pi i}{2}x(x-Q)}S_b(x).}

nodes.name: Integral form of $G_b(z)$
nodes.statement: For $0\leq Re(z)\leq Q$, $G_b(z)$ can be expressed as \Eq{ G_b(x)=\over[\ze_b]\exp\left(-\int_{\W}\frac{e^{\pi tz}}{(e^{\pi bt}-1)(e^{\pi b\inv t}-1)}\frac{dt}{t}\right),} where \Eq{\ze_b=e^{\frac{\pi i}{2}(\frac{b^2+b^{-2}}{6}+\frac{1}{2})},} and the contour goes along $\R$ with a small semicircle going above the pole at $t=0$. The integral converges absolutely for $0<Re(z)<Q$ and conditionally at the boundary.
nodes.statement_short: In the strip $0\leq Re(z)\leq Q$, $G_b$ has a convergent contour-integral representation.
conclusions: the contour goes along $\R$ with a small semicircle going above the pole at $t=0$
The integral converges absolutely for $0<Re(z)<Q$ and conditionally at the boundary.

nodes.name: Meromorphic continuation, zeros and poles of $G_b$ and $S_b$
nodes.statement: The function $G_b$ and $S_b$ can be analytic continued to the whole complex plane as a meromorphic function, so that they have simple zeros at $z=Q+nb+mb\inv$ and simple poles at $z=-nb+-mb\inv$ for $n,m\in \Z_{\geq 0}$.
nodes.statement_short: $G_b,S_b$ extend meromorphically with simple zeros at $Q+nb+mb\inv$ and simple poles at $-nb-mb\inv$.
conclusions: The function $G_b$ and $S_b$ can be analytic continued to the whole complex plane as a meromorphic function
they have simple zeros at $z=Q+nb+mb\inv$ and simple poles at $z=-nb+-mb\inv$

nodes.name: Self-duality of $S_b$ and $G_b$
nodes.statement: Self-duality: \Eq{S_b(x)=S_{b\inv}(x),\tab G_b(x)=G_{b\inv}(x).}
nodes.statement_short: Both $S_b$ and $G_b$ are invariant under $b\leftrightarrow b\inv$.

nodes.name: Functional equations of $S_b$ and $G_b$
nodes.statement: Functional equations: \Eq{S_b(x+b^{\pm1})=2\sin(\pi b^{\pm1}x)S_b(x),\tab G_b(x+b^{\pm 1})=(1-e^{2\pi ib^{\pm 1}x})G_b(x).}
nodes.statement_short: Shifting the argument by $b^{\pm1}$ multiplies $S_b$ by $2\sin(\pi b^{\pm1}x)$ and $G_b$ by $(1-e^{2\pi ib^{\pm1}x})$.

nodes.name: Reflection property
nodes.statement: Reflection property: \Eq{S_b(x)S_b(Q-x)=1,\tab G_b(x)G_b(Q-x)=e^{\pi ix(x-Q)}.}
nodes.statement_short: Reflection about $Q/2$: $S_b(x)S_b(Q-x)=1$ and $G_b(x)G_b(Q-x)=e^{\pi ix(x-Q)}$.

nodes.name: Complex conjugation property
nodes.statement: Complex conjugation: \Eq{\overline{S_b(x)}=\frac{1}{S_b(Q-\over[x])},\tab \overline{G_b(x)}=\frac{1}{G_b(Q-\bar{x})},} in particular \Eq{\left|S_b(\frac{Q}{2}+ix)\right|=\left|G_b(\frac{Q}{2}+ix)\right|=1 \mbox{ for $x\in\R$}.}
nodes.statement_short: Conjugation inverts the value at the reflected point; hence modulus 1 on the line $Re(z)=Q/2$.

nodes.name: Asymptotic properties of $G_b$
nodes.statement: Asymptotic properties: \Eq{G_b(x)\sim\left\{\begin{array}{cc}\bar{\ze_b}&Im(x)\to+\oo,\\\ze_b e^{\pi ix(x-Q)}&Im(x)\to-\oo,\end{array}\right.} where \Eq{\ze_b=e^{\frac{\pi i}{4}+\frac{\pi i}{12}(b^2+b^{-2})}.}
nodes.statement_short: $G_b$ tends to the constant $\bar{\ze_b}$ upward and grows like $\ze_b e^{\pi ix(x-Q)}$ downward.

nodes.name: Residues of $G_b$
nodes.statement: Residues: \Eq{\lim_{x\to 0} xG_b(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi},} or more generally, \Eq{Res\frac{1}{G_b(Q+z)}=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\prod_{k=1}^n(1-q^{2k})\inv\prod_{l=1}^m(1-\widetilde{q}^{2l})\inv} at $z=nb+mb\inv, n,m\in\Z_{\geq0}$ and $\widetilde{q}=e^{\pi i b^{-2}}$.
nodes.statement_short: The pole of $G_b$ at $0$ has residue $1/2\pi$, with a $q$-product formula for the general residue.

nodes.name: Extension of $G_b$ by $nQ$-shifts
nodes.statement: Using the functional equation \eqref{funceq}, the function can be extended to the whole complex plane using the integral formula \eqref{intform} by \Eq{G_b(z+nQ)=G_b(x)\prod_{k=1}^n (1-e^{2\pi ib(z+(k-1)Q)}),} \Eq{G_b(z-nQ)=G_b(x)\prod_{k=1}^n (1-e^{2\pi ib(z-kQ)})\inv,} where $n\in \Z_{\geq 0}$, $0\leq Re(z)\leq Q$.
nodes.statement_short: Iterating the functional equation extends the strip formula to all of $\C$ by finite products.

nodes.name: Symmetry axis and apparent multiple poles for $b=0.7$
nodes.statement: We observe the symmetry along the axis $Re(z)=\frac{Q}{2}$, governed by the reflection properties \eqref{reflection}. Furthermore, the poles and zeros along $Im(z)=0$ are supposed to be simple, by comparing with the graph of $f(z)=z$ given in Section \ref{sec:complex}. The appearance of certain double or triple poles and zeros for the graph $b=0.7$ comes from the fact that $b\inv\simeq1.43\sim 2b$, hence certain multiples $nb+mb\inv$ will come close together. For example, $z=2b+2b\inv=4.257$ and $z=4b+b\inv=4.229$.
nodes.statement_short: The graph is symmetric about $Re(z)=Q/2$; apparent multiple poles at $b=0.7$ are near-coincident simple ones.

nodes.name: Exponential decay and growth in the negative imaginary direction
nodes.statement: It has exponential decay along the negative imaginary direction for $Re(z)<\frac{Q}{2}$, and exponential growth for $Re(z)>\frac{Q}{2}$. According to the asymptotic behavior from the last section, the growth is given by \Eq{|G_b(s+it)| = e^{-\pi t(2s-Q)},\tab t\to -\oo.} This also explains the brightness for different $b$ when $Im(z)\to -\oo$.
nodes.statement_short: Modulus behaves like $e^{-\pi t(2s-Q)}$ as $t\to-\oo$, decaying left of $Re(z)=Q/2$ and growing right of it.

nodes.name: Limit in the positive imaginary direction
nodes.statement: On the other hand, it approaches the limit $\overline{\ze}_b = e^{\pi i(b^2+b^-2+3)/12}$ in the positive imaginary direction.

nodes.name: Phase change along $Re(z)=\frac{Q}{2}$
nodes.statement: We observe the phase change along any given direction. In particular along $Re(z)=\frac{Q}{2}$ we do have the changes given according to $e^{\pi iz^2}$, increasing in frequency as $Im(z)\to -\oo$.

nodes.name: Resemblance to the Riemann Zeta function
nodes.statement: Finally let us note the similar shape compared with the Riemann Zeta function, which we believe is a coincidence.

nodes.name: The limiting case $b=1$
nodes.statement: For the case $b=1$, from Figure \ref{Gx1} we observe that the successive poles and zeroes have increasing order, due to the fact that $b$ and $b\inv$ coincide, which creates multiple poles. The poles at $z=-n$ and the zeroes at $z=2+n$ both have order $n+1$ for $n=0,1,2,...$
nodes.statement_short: At $b=1$ the coinciding lattices $nb+mb\inv$ merge, giving poles and zeroes of order $n+1$.

nodes.name: Full symmetry of the graph of $S_b(z)$
nodes.statement: The graph can be made symmetric by considering $S_b(z)$ instead. The reflection properties give \Eq{S_b(z)=S_b(Q-z)\inv,\tab \over[S_b(z)]=S_b(\over[z]),} suggesting a full symmetry of the graph along $Re(z)=\frac{Q}{2}$ and $Im(z)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Reflection and conjugation make the $S_b$ graph symmetric about both $Re(z)=Q/2$ and the real axis.
conclusions: a full symmetry of the graph along $Re(z)=\frac{Q}{2}$ and $Im(z)=0$

nodes.name: $S_b(z)$ is real on the real line
nodes.statement: Since we know that $\over[S_b(z)]=S_b(\over[z])$, we conclude that $S_b(z)$ takes real values when $z$ is real. Therefore it suffices to plot the graphs for $S_b(z)$, and the values for $G_b(z)$ just amount to a phase change by the factor $e^{\pi iz(z-Q)/2}$ (cf. \eqref{GS}).
nodes.statement_short: Conjugation symmetry forces $S_b$ to be real-valued on $\R$, so $G_b$ differs only by a phase.
conclusions: $S_b(z)$ takes real values when $z$ is real
the values for $G_b(z)$ just amount to a phase change by the factor $e^{\pi iz(z-Q)/2}$

nodes.name: Numerical overflow for small $b$
nodes.statement: Here we plot the graph for $b=0.7, b=0.248$ as well as the limiting case $b=0.1$. Mathematica obtains a numerical overflow beyond this small value of $b$ due to large exponential appearing in the integration of the definition, and the function is expected to be quite badly behaved as the examples show.

nodes.name: Simplicity of the zeroes on the real line
nodes.statement: We can clearly observe the locations of the poles and zeroes. The zeroes are simple from the fact that the values of the function should alternate in signs. For $b=0.7$, the appearance of a seemingly critical points comes from the fact that $b\inv = 1.429$ is quite close to $2b=1.4$ as explained before.
nodes.statement_short: Sign alternation shows the real zeroes are simple; $b=0.7$ artefacts come from $b\inv\approx 2b$.

nodes.name: Amplitude recursion and $\ln 2$ shift of the log plot
nodes.statement: By the functional equation \eqref{funceq}, the whole graph really depends on the portion $0<x<Q$. The size of the bump governs the recurring amplitude of the graph by successive factor of 2, which comes from $2\sin(\pi b)\sin(\pi b\inv)$ appearing in the reflection properties for $S_b(x)$. This also explains the "periodicity" of the log plot for $b=0.1$, which, in fact, has shifted by $\ln(2)$.
nodes.statement_short: The functional equation reduces the graph to $0<x<Q$ and explains the $\ln 2$ shift of the log plot.

nodes.name: Shape of the bump on $0<x<Q$
nodes.statement: The portion of the graph $0<x<Q$ has exactly one local minimum and one local maximum for all values of $b$, and they are all positive real numbers. By taking the log plot in Figure \ref{logSQx}, which essentially is the value of the integral, (we rescaled so that the endpoints at $x=0$ and $x=Q$ matches), we see immediately that the size of the bump has a symmetric exponential relation along $x=\frac{Q}{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: On $0<x<Q$ there is exactly one local max and min, with the bump size symmetric about $x=Q/2$.

nodes.name: Common limit $\over[\ze_b]$ along the imaginary direction
nodes.statement: We observe the asymptotic behavior, that as $x\to \oo$, they all approach the complex number $\over[\ze_b]=0.123-0.992i$.

nodes.name: Growth of $|G_b(ix)|$ and $|G_b(Q+ix)|$
nodes.statement: For $x\to-\oo$, $|G_b(ix)|\to e^{\pi Qx}$, while $|G_b(Q+ix)|\to e^{-\pi Qx}$. The relationship of the two graphs can easily be derived from the reflection properties \eqref{reflection}.

nodes.name: Unimodularity and quadratic phase on $Re(z)=\frac{Q}{2}$
nodes.statement: Finally $|G_b(\frac{Q}{2}+ix)|=1$, and the asymptotic behavior for $x\to-\oo$ is $\overline{\ze_b}e^{-\pi i\frac{Q^2}{4}}e^{-\pi ix^2}$, hence the increase in frequency is governed by $\pi x^2$.

nodes.name: Compact quantum dilogarithm
nodes.statement: The analytic properties extend to the compact case, when $Im(b^2)>0$, using an infinite product expansion, which we will call it the \emph{compact quantum dilogarithm}:
nodes.genus: quantum dilogarithm given by an infinite product expansion

nodes.name: Infinite product description of $G_b$
nodes.statement: \cite[Prop 5]{Sh} For $Im(b^2)>0$, we have the infinite product descripiton \Eq{G_b(z)=\bar{\ze_b}\frac{\prod_{n=1}^\oo (1-e^{2\pi ib\inv(x-nb\inv)})}{\prod_{n=0}^\oo(1-e^{2\pi ib(x+nb)})}.}
nodes.statement_short: For $Im(b^2)>0$, $G_b$ equals $\bar{\ze_b}$ times a ratio of two convergent infinite products.

nodes.name: Poles and zeroes in the compact case
nodes.statement: The location of the poles and zeroes are still the same, with poles at $-nb-mb\inv$, and zeroes at $Q+nb+mb\inv$ for $n,m=0,1,2,...$

nodes.name: The case $b^2=ir$
nodes.statement: The most interesting case occurs when $b^2=ir$ for $r>0$, in which $0<q=e^{\pi ib^2}<1$. We establish the graph for $b=e^{\pi i/4}0.7$ in Figure \ref{Gx07i}

nodes.name: Quadratic exponential growth in the compact case
nodes.statement: We have highlighted the zeroes with black dots and poles with white dots that align nicely together. We observe that the exponential decay and growth are extremely fast, due to the asymmetry bringing in a real part for the asymptotic $e^{\pi iz(z-Q)}$, thus giving a quadratic exponential growth.
nodes.statement_short: Complex $b$ gives the asymptotic $e^{\pi iz(z-Q)}$ a real part, producing quadratic exponential growth.

nodes.name: The case $b=e^{\pi i/4}0.248$
nodes.statement: The case for $b=e^{\pi i/4}0.248$ illustrated in Figure \ref{Gx0248i} is less interesting due to the quick growth and decay of the function.

nodes.name: Separation of poles for smaller $|b|$
nodes.statement: We observe that the separation of the poles is stretching out with increased exponential decay/growth compared with bigger $|b|$.

nodes.name: Limit of $G_b$ to the classical Gamma function
nodes.statement: The following limit holds for $b^2=ir\to i0^+$ \Eq{\lim_{r\to 0} \frac{G_b(bz)}{\sqrt{-i}|b| (1-q^2)^{x-1}} = \G(z),} where $\sqrt{-i}=e^{-\frac{\pi i}{4}}$ and $-\frac{\pi}{2}<\arg(1-q^2)<\frac{\pi}{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Suitably normalized, $G_b(bz)$ converges to the classical Gamma function $\G(z)$ as $b^2=ir\to i0^+$.

nodes.name: The modified function $\til[G]_b(z)$
nodes.statement: Let us demonstrate the limiting process by considering the graph of the above function \Eq{\til[G]_b(z):=\frac{G_b(bz)}{\sqrt{-i}|b| (1-q^2)^{z-1}}.}

nodes.name: Alignment of poles and zeroes of $\til[G]_b$
nodes.statement: From Figure \ref{GG07}, we see that under multiplication by $b$ in the argument, the zeroes and poles are aligned with the axis. The first zero occur at $z=\frac{Q}{b}=1-\frac{1}{|b|^2}i$. Now as $|b|\to 0$, we see that $\frac{Q}{b}$ moves downward and pushes away the zeroes and poles. It becomes clear in the graph for smaller $|b|$.
nodes.statement_short: Rescaling by $b$ aligns poles/zeroes with the axis and pushes the first zero $Q/b$ downward as $|b|\to0$.

nodes.name: Graphical demonstration of the Gamma limit
nodes.statement: Now as $|b|$ becomes smaller, from Figure \ref{GG035} we see that the small area around center begins to take shape with the poles and zeroes pushed away. Further reducing $|b|$ so that $\frac{Q}{b}$ is out of plotting range, we can see immediately in Figure \ref{GG0248} that indeed the graph resembles the Gamma function $\G(z)$ given in Figure \ref{Gamma}.
nodes.statement_short: For small $|b|$ the plotted $\til[G]_b$ visually converges to the Gamma function graph.

nodes.name: All variants are shifts, scalings and inverses of $G_b$
nodes.statement: We will see below that all variants of $G_b$ amounts to shifting, scaling, taking inverses and multiplication by a constant. Hence the graphs of these variants can be obtained from those of $G_b(z)$ easily by shifting, stretching, and color phase changes.
nodes.statement_short: Every literature variant of the quantum dilogarithm is an elementary transform of $G_b$, so its graph follows.
conclusions: all variants of $G_b$ amounts to shifting, scaling, taking inverses and multiplication by a constant
the graphs of these variants can be obtained from those of $G_b(z)$ easily by shifting, stretching, and color phase changes

nodes.name: The function $g_b(z)$
nodes.statement: The important function that satisfies the pentagon equation for Weyl-type operator is defined by \Eq{g_b(z)=\frac{\over[\ze_b]}{G_b(\frac{Q}{2}+\frac{\log z}{2\pi ib})}.}
nodes.genus: The important function that satisfies the pentagon equation for Weyl-type operator

nodes.name: Quantum exponential and pentagon relations for $g_b$
nodes.statement: Let $u, v$ be positive self-adjoint operators with $uv=q^2vu$, $q=e^{\pi i b^2}$. Then \Eq{g_b(u)g_b(v)=g_b(u+v),} \Eq{g_b(v)g_b(u)=g_b(u)g_b(q\inv uv)g_b(v).}
nodes.statement_short: $g_b$ satisfies the $q$-exponential law and the quantum pentagon identity on Weyl-type operators.
assumptions: Let $u, v$ be positive self-adjoint operators with $uv=q^2vu$, $q=e^{\pi i b^2}$

nodes.name: Branch cut and range of the argument of $g_b$
nodes.statement: However, the graph of $g_b$ which carries a branch cut at $x\in(-\oo,0)$ is not particularly interesting, due to slow growth, and the fact that $-\pi < Im(\log z)<\pi$, so that \Eq{0<\frac{Q}{2}-\frac{1}{2b}<Re(\frac{Q}{2}+\frac{\log z}{2\pi ib}) < \frac{Q}{2}+\frac{1}{2b}<Q,} and hence the argument in $G_b$ never hits any zeroes or poles.
nodes.statement_short: The logarithm confines the argument of $G_b$ to the strip $0<Re<Q$, so $g_b$ has no zeroes or poles.

nodes.name: Analytic continuation in $b$ and the compact expansion
nodes.statement: The quantum dilogarithm $G_ b(x)$ defined above has real $b$ as parameters. Although the integral formula can be analytically continued to complex $b$ with positive real part, we recall that the function coincide with the \emph{compact quantum dilogarithm} given in Prop \ref{infprod}: \Eq{G_b(z)=\bar{\ze_b}\frac{\prod_{n=1}^\oo (1-e^{2\pi ib\inv(x-nb\inv)})}{\prod_{n=0}^\oo(1-e^{2\pi ib(x+nb)})}.}
nodes.statement_short: For complex $b$ with positive real part the integral formula agrees with the infinite product expansion.

nodes.name: Volkov's hyperbolic Gamma function $\c(z)$
nodes.statement: Let $q=e^{\pi i\t}$ for $Im(\t)>0$. Then the hyperbolic Gamma function is defined by \Eq{\c(z):=\frac{(q^2e^{-2\pi iz};q^2)_\oo}{(e^{-2\pi iz/\t};q^{-2/\t^2})_\oo}.}

nodes.name: Relation between $\c(z)$ and $G_b$
nodes.statement: With $\t=b^2$, we have \Eq{\c(z)=\over[\ze_b]G_b(Q-\frac{z}{b})\inv.}

nodes.name: Faddeev's quantum dilogarithm $\psi(p)$
nodes.statement: Let $s_q(w)=\prod_{n=0}^\oo (1+q^{2n+1}w)$ and define \Eq{\psi(p):=\frac{s_q(e^{bp})}{s_{\til[q]}(e^{p/b})},} where $\til[q]=e^{\pi ib^{-2}}$. Then $\psi(p)$ admits the integral expansion \Eq{\psi(p):=\exp\left(\frac{1}{4}\int_\W \frac{e^{ip\xi/\pi}}{\sinh(b\xi)\sinh(\xi/b)}\frac{d\xi}{\xi}\right).}
nodes.statement_short: Faddeev's $\psi$ as a ratio of $q$-products, with an equivalent contour-integral expansion.

nodes.name: Fock-Goncharov's $\Phi^{\hbar}(z)$
nodes.statement: \Eq{\Phi^{\hbar}(z):=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{4}\int_\W \frac{e^{-ipz}}{\sinh(\pi p)\sinh(\pi \hbar p)}\frac{dp}{p}\right),}

nodes.name: Woronowicz-Zakrzewski's $V_\h(z)$
nodes.statement: \Eq{V_\h(z):=\exp\left(\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_0^\oo \log(1+x^{-\h})\frac{dx}{x+e^{-z}}\right).}

nodes.name: Relations between $V_\h$, $\Phi^{\hbar}$, $\psi$, $g_b$ and $G_b$
nodes.statement: \Eq{V_{b^{-2}}(z)=\Phi^{b^2}(z)=g_b(e^{z})\inv=\ze_bG_b\left(\frac{Q}{2}-\frac{iz}{2\pi b}\right),} \Eq{\psi(z)=\Phi^{b^2}(-bz)\inv=\c(b(Q+\frac{z}{2\pi i}))=\over[\ze_b]G_b(\frac{Q}{2}+\frac{iz}{2\pi})\inv.}
nodes.statement_short: All of $V_\h$, $\Phi^{\hbar}$, $\psi$ and $g_b$ are shifted, scaled or inverted copies of $G_b$.

nodes.name: Ruijinaars's G function $G(a_+,a_-;z)$
nodes.statement: Let $a_-,a_+$ be two positive real numbers. Ruijinaars's G function is defined by \Eq{G(a_+,a_-;z):=\exp\left(i\int_0^\oo \frac{dy}{y}\left(\frac{\sin 2yz}{2\sinh(a_+y)\sinh(a_-y)}-\frac{z}{a_+a_-y}\right)\right),} with $|Im(z)|<(a_++a_-)/2$ and extend meromorphically to the whole complex plane.
nodes.statement_short: Two-parameter hyperbolic G function defined by an integral in the strip $|Im(z)|<(a_++a_-)/2$.
differentia: $|Im(z)|<(a_++a_-)/2$ and extend meromorphically to the whole complex plane

nodes.name: Ruijinaars's G function in terms of $S_b$
nodes.statement: Then \Eq{G(b,b\inv;z)=S_b(\frac{Q}{2}-iz).}
assumptions: Let $a_-,a_+$ be two positive real numbers
